456.title: She loved much (Luke 7:36–50)
456.hook: a sinful woman washes his feet with tears at a dinner she wasn't invited to
456.howItsDone: Catholics connect this story with the sacrament of Penance, where sins are forgiven and the priest sends the penitent away in peace, and some pray with it as an examination of how much they have been forgiven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a funeral stopped at the gate of Naim, and a mother got her son back. Your line was weep not. Who did you comfort? Day four hundred fifty-six, and a new week.

A dinner party in a nice house. The host is a Pharisee named Simon, who has asked the new teacher everyone is talking about to eat with him. The guests aren't sitting on chairs. They're reclining on couches, leaning on one elbow, feet stretched out behind them. And someone comes in who was never asked. A woman of the city, known as a sinner, walks in carrying an alabaster jar of ointment. She hasn't been invited. She goes straight to the teacher's feet. Today, what she does there, and what he says about it.
screen: `A DINNER AT SIMON'S HOUSE.` → `GUESTS RECLINING, FEET BEHIND.` → `AN UNINVITED WOMAN WITH A JAR.`

segments.voice: She stands behind him, at his feet, and starts to cry. Her tears fall on his feet, so she wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and pours out the ointment. Simon thinks to himself: if this man were a prophet, he'd know what sort of woman is touching him. Jesus answers the thought with a story. Two men owe a lender money, one five hundred pence, one fifty. Neither can pay, so he forgives them both. Which will love him more? Simon answers, carefully: I suppose the one who was forgiven more. Right, says Jesus. Then he turns toward the woman but keeps talking to Simon. You gave me no water for my feet; she washed them with tears. You gave me no kiss; she hasn't stopped kissing my feet. You didn't anoint my head; she anointed my feet. And then the line: "Many sins are forgiven her, because she hath loved much. But to whom less is forgiven, he loveth less." To her he says: "Thy faith hath made thee safe, go in peace." Simon isn't the villain here. He invited Jesus, listened, and answered honestly. The story is about two kinds of guests, and it asks which one we are. Luke never names the woman. For many centuries in the Western Church, following a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great, she was identified with Mary Magdalene. The Church's calendar today no longer joins them, and the Gospel itself never says. What Luke does say is that she loved much, and that Jesus sent her away forgiven, in peace.
screen: `TEARS, HAIR, KISSES, OINTMENT.` · `TWO DEBTORS, BOTH FORGIVEN.` · `NO WATER, NO KISS, NO OIL.` · `GO IN PEACE.` · then, large: `SHE HATH LOVED MUCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love without counting. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've been forgiven: by God, if you pray, or by a friend, a parent, a partner who let something go. Remember how it felt when they didn't hold it over you. Let that settle in your body. Then think of one person you've been loving carefully, in measured amounts, keeping track. Picture giving them one thing today without counting: a kindness, an apology, an hour. If you pray, you can thank God for what you've been forgiven. The bell holds the time.
Alabaster. The jar of ointment the unnamed woman poured on Jesus' feet at Simon's dinner, her tears showing how much she knew she'd been forgiven. Today's word.
Your line: go in peace. Today, give one kindness to someone without keeping track of what they owe you. Day four hundred fifty-six.

screen: `DAY 456 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WOMEN WHO FUNDED HIM.`

457.title: The women who funded him (Luke 8:1–3)
457.hook: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others ministered to him of their substance
457.howItsDone: The Church keeps the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene on July 22, and in many Catholic parishes women carry much of the daily work: catechesis, sacristy care, charity, music and administration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman with an alabaster jar at Simon's dinner. Your line was go in peace. Did you love without counting? Day four hundred fifty-seven.

Here's a question the Gospels don't usually stop to answer: who paid for all this? Jesus and twelve men walking from town to town, for months, not fishing, not farming, not working for wages. Somebody bought the bread. Somebody paid for sandals and oil and a roof when there was one. Most of the time the Gospels skip the budget. Luke doesn't. In three short verses, tucked between bigger stories, he tells us exactly who kept the whole mission going. Today, the names.
screen: `WHO PAID FOR ALL THIS?` → `THIRTEEN MEN, NO WAGES.` → `THREE VERSES WITH THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Luke says Jesus went through the cities and towns preaching the kingdom, and the twelve were with him, and certain women. Then he names them. Mary, called Magdalene, out of whom seven devils had gone. Joanna, wife of Chusa, Herod's steward: a woman married to a man who managed the household of the king who would later mock Jesus. Susanna, about whom we know nothing else at all. And "many others who ministered unto him of their substance." Their substance means their own money and goods. These women weren't just along for the ride. They were paying for it. And ministered is a word worth stopping on. In Greek it's the verb diakoneo, to serve, the same root that gives the Church the word deacon. Luke uses it here for women who serve with what they own. Now follow these same women forward. Luke says the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance and watched the crucifixion. They saw where he was laid. And on Sunday morning, Mary Magdalene and Joanna are named among the women who found the tomb empty and told the apostles. The ones who funded the road were the ones still there at the end. The Church remembers this. In 2016 Pope Francis raised the memorial of Mary Magdalene to a feast, and the decree honored her with an old title: apostle to the apostles. Many parishes still run on people like Joanna and Susanna, often women, often unnamed: the ones who count the collection, wash the linens, teach the children, and bring the casseroles. Luke wrote their names down.
screen: `MARY, JOANNA, SUSANNA, MANY OTHERS.` · `OF THEIR SUBSTANCE: THEIR OWN MONEY.` · `MINISTERED: THE DEACON WORD.` · `THE SAME WOMEN AT THE TOMB.` · then, large: `THEY MINISTERED OF THEIR SUBSTANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank the women who carry your parish, or your community. Settle, and breathe. Picture the place you belong: a parish, a school, a team, a family. Now look for the ones doing the work nobody announces. The woman who unlocks the door. The one who makes the coffee, keeps the list, remembers the birthdays. Pick one. Think of exactly what she gives. Decide how you'll thank her this week, by name, for something specific. If you pray, thank God for her. The bell holds the time.
Mary Magdalene. Named first among the women who funded Jesus' mission out of their own means, and stayed to the end, even at the tomb. Today's word.
Your line: they ministered of their substance. Today, thank one woman who carries something for your community, and say exactly what. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

458.title: Take nothing (Luke 9:1–17)
458.hook: the twelve sent out light, then five thousand fed
458.howItsDone: Catholics hear the feeding of the five thousand from Luke on the solemnity of the Body and Blood of Christ in the year of Luke's Gospel, and some religious orders vowed to poverty take the mission of the twelve as part of their pattern of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene and the women who paid for the road and stayed to the end. Your line was they ministered of their substance. Who did you thank? Day four hundred fifty-eight.

The charger, the spare charger, the snacks, the just-in-case jacket, the bag that won't close. That's packing for a weekend. Now take a mission instead: go to towns you've never seen, heal the sick, preach the kingdom of God. And the packing list comes back mostly crossed out. That's chapter nine of Luke. The twelve are sent out on their own. And when they come back, there's a hungry crowd of thousands and almost no food. Today, two scenes about having nothing.
screen: `THE BAG THAT WON'T CLOSE.` → `A PACKING LIST, CROSSED OUT.` → `TWO SCENES ABOUT HAVING NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Jesus gives the twelve power over devils and diseases, and then the list: "Take nothing for your journey; neither staff, nor scrip, nor bread, nor money; neither have two coats." A scrip is a traveler's bag, the kind you'd carry food in. No bag, no bread, no cash, no spare clothes. Stay in whatever house takes you in. If a town won't receive you, shake the dust off your feet and move on. Why so little? Luke doesn't say. One way to read it: traveling light means depending on others. The twelve have to knock on doors and be received. Their poverty makes room for someone else's welcome. And it works. Luke says they went through the towns preaching and healing everywhere. Then they come back, and Jesus takes them aside to a desert place near Bethsaida, and the crowds follow. Evening comes. The twelve make the practical suggestion: send them away to find food and lodging. Jesus answers: "Give you them to eat." They count what they have: five loaves and two fishes, and about five thousand men. And here Luke slows down. Jesus takes the bread, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives to the disciples to set before the crowd. Took, blessed, broke, gave. Catholics hear nearly the same movements at every Mass, in the words of the Last Supper. Everyone eats and is filled, and twelve baskets of fragments are gathered up, from what the twelve had called too little. The two scenes belong together. First the twelve learn to go out with nothing. Then they learn that what little they have, placed in his hands, is enough to feed a crowd.
screen: `NO STAFF, NO BAG, NO BREAD, NO MONEY.` · `TRAVELING LIGHT MAKES ROOM FOR WELCOME.` · `GIVE YOU THEM TO EAT.` · `TOOK, BLESSED, BROKE, GAVE.` · then, large: `TWELVE BASKETS LEFT OVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go through today lighter. Settle, and breathe. Picture what you're carrying into today. Not just in your bag. The grudge, the five worries, the backup plan for the backup plan. Pick one thing you can set down for the day. It might be literal: leave your phone in another room for an hour. It might be inside: one worry you hand over. Imagine setting it on a table and walking out the door without it. If you pray, you can place it in God's hands, like the five loaves. The bell holds the time.
Take nothing. Jesus' packing list for the twelve: no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, so they'd depend on welcome, and then learn that a little is enough. Today's word.
Your line: nothing for the journey. Today, leave one thing behind on purpose, and notice who or what fills the space. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

459.title: He set his face (Luke 9:51–62)
459.hook: he turns toward Jerusalem, and the foxes have holes
459.howItsDone: Catholics hear this passage at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel; the Catechism teaches that family ties matter but are not absolute, and that following Jesus comes first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve sent out with nothing, and five loaves for five thousand. Your line was nothing for the journey. What did you leave behind? Day four hundred fifty-nine.

Partway through Luke's Gospel, the book turns. Until now Jesus has been moving around Galilee: the lake, the villages, the hills. Then, in one verse, he turns toward Jerusalem. From here on, Luke tells the story as one long walk to the city where, as Jesus has already told his disciples, he will suffer. Readers call this stretch the travel narrative. And the very first thing that happens on the road is a door shut in his face. Today, the turn.
screen: `IN ONE VERSE, THE BOOK TURNS.` → `ONE LONG WALK TO JERUSALEM.` → `A DOOR SHUTS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the hinge in the Douay-Rheims: "And it came to pass, when the days of his assumption were accomplishing, that he steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem." Assumption here means his being taken up, to the cross and to the Father. To set your face is an old Hebrew way of speaking: to fix your direction and refuse to be turned. Isaiah's servant says he has set his face hard as rock. Jesus sends messengers ahead into a Samaritan village, and the village won't receive him, because he's headed for Jerusalem. James and John ask if they should call fire down from heaven. Jesus turns and rebukes them, and they simply go on to another village. Then three people meet him on the road. The first says, I'll follow you wherever you go. Jesus answers: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Know what you're signing up for. The second says, let me first go and bury my father. The third says, let me first say goodbye at home. And Jesus answers with a farmer's picture: "No man putting his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God." Anyone who has plowed knows why. If you look over your shoulder, the furrow wanders. These sayings are hard, and Luke doesn't soften them. The Church reads them not as contempt for family, which the commandments honor, but as a question of what comes first. Jesus has set his face. He asks the people walking beside him to set theirs.
screen: `THE DAYS OF HIS ASSUMPTION.` · `NO FIRE ON THE SAMARITAN VILLAGE.` · `THE FOXES HAVE HOLES.` · `A HAND ON THE PLOW.` · then, large: `HE STEADFASTLY SET HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: commit to one hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been circling: a conversation you keep postponing, a habit you keep almost starting, a decision you keep reopening. Pick one. Now picture yourself setting your face toward it, the way you'd turn to walk a road. What's the first step, today? Name it. Notice the urge to look back, the reasons to wait. Let them be there, and keep facing forward. If you pray, ask for steadiness. The bell holds the time.
assumption. Luke's word for Jesus being taken up, to the cross and to the Father, the hinge where he fixed his face toward Jerusalem. Today's word.
Your line: no looking back. Today, take the first step on your one hard thing, and when you want to turn around, keep your hand on the plow. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

460.title: The seventy-two (Luke 10:1–24)
460.hook: sent in pairs like lambs among wolves, peace to this house
460.howItsDone: Some Catholic families bless their homes at Epiphany by chalking the year and the letters C+M+B over the door, and the traditional rite for blessing a house opens with Jesus' words, peace be to this house.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus' assumption drew near as he set his face toward Jerusalem, and the foxes had holes. Your line was no looking back. Did you take the first step? Day four hundred sixty.

In some Catholic homes, around the Epiphany in January, someone climbs on a chair with a piece of blessed chalk and writes over the front door: the year, split in two, with three letters in the middle, C, M and B, joined by crosses. People read the letters as the names tradition gives the three wise men, and also as the start of a Latin blessing: may Christ bless this house. Guests walk under it all year. It's a small, homemade custom. The wish in it is much older: on a road in Luke, Jesus sends out a wider circle of disciples and tells them the first thing to say at every door. Today, the seventy-two.
screen: `CHALK OVER THE FRONT DOOR.` → `MAY CHRIST BLESS THIS HOUSE.` → `THE FIRST THING TO SAY AT A DOOR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday he set his face toward Jerusalem. Now he sends people ahead of him. Not just the twelve this time. The Douay-Rheims says the Lord appointed "other seventy-two: and he sent them two and two before his face into every city and place whither he himself was to come." Two and two, so nobody goes alone. Then the honest warning: "behold I send you as lambs among wolves." No purse, no bag, no sandals, no stopping to chat on the road. And at every door, one sentence first: "Into whatsoever house you enter, first say: Peace be to this house." If a son of peace is there, Jesus says, your peace will rest on him. If not, it will come back to you. You can't waste a blessing. It either lands or returns. Behind the Gospel's word for peace stands the Hebrew shalom: not just quiet, but wholeness, everything as it should be. The number is a small puzzle: some Bibles say seventy here, and the Douay says seventy-two. Some readers connect it with the list of the world's nations in Genesis chapter ten, and hear in it a message meant for everyone. And the ending is pure joy. The seventy-two come back thrilled: even the devils obey us! Jesus says rejoice in something better, that your names are written in heaven. These aren't the twelve. They're a wider circle of disciples, sent two by two, with peace as their first word.
screen: `TWO AND TWO, BEFORE HIS FACE.` · `LAMBS AMONG WOLVES.` · `A BLESSING LANDS OR RETURNS.` · `SEVENTY OR SEVENTY-TWO.` · then, large: `PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless a house you enter. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next door you'll walk through today: your own front door, an office, a classroom, a friend's apartment, a hospital room. Picture yourself at its threshold. Before you step in, imagine wishing peace on everyone inside, the ones you love and the ones you don't. You don't need to say it aloud. If you pray, you can say Jesus' own words silently: peace be to this house. Then picture walking in lighter. The bell holds the time.
The seventy-two. The wider circle of disciples Jesus sent out two by two, as lambs among wolves, with peace as their first word at every door. Today's word.
Your line: peace be to this house. Today, say it silently at every threshold you cross, and watch where it lands. Day four hundred sixty.

461.title: Teach us to pray (Luke 11:1–13)
461.hook: the Our Father, a friend at midnight, ask, seek, knock
461.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Our Father at every Mass and at the start of each decade of the rosary; the Catechism devotes its final section to the prayer, comparing Luke's five petitions with Matthew's seven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventy-two went out two by two with one sentence for every door. Your line was peace be to this house. Where did it land? Day four hundred sixty-one.

It's midnight. A friend of yours has shown up after a long trip, hungry, and your kitchen is empty. Not a crust. So you walk next door and knock. From inside, your neighbor groans: the door's locked, the kids are asleep in the bed with me, I can't get up. You knock again. Jesus tells this little comedy right after his disciples ask him for something. Today, what they asked, and why he answers with a man knocking at midnight.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, AN EMPTY KITCHEN.` → `THE KIDS ARE ASLEEP. GO AWAY.` → `YOU KNOCK AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Luke sets the scene simply. Jesus is praying somewhere, and when he stops, one of his disciples says: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." John had given his followers a way to pray. Now Jesus gives his. Luke's version of the Our Father is shorter than Matthew's, the one Catholics say at Mass. The Catechism notes the difference: Luke gives five petitions, Matthew seven. Luke's begins simply with Father, then hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, give us our daily bread, forgive us our sins as we forgive, and lead us not into temptation. Then, right away, the midnight friend. Jesus says: even if the neighbor won't get up because you're his friend, "yet, because of his importunity, he will rise, and give him as many as he needeth." Importunity means pestering. The Greek word is even bolder: shamelessness. The man gets bread because he won't stop knocking. Then the promise: "Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you." And one last picture: which father, if his son asks for a fish, hands him a snake? If you, imperfect as you are, give good things to your children, how much more will the Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him. Notice where the promise ends. Not with whatever you ask for, but with the good Spirit. In Luke, prayer looks like shameless knocking at the door of a Father who wants to give.
screen: `LORD, TEACH US TO PRAY.` · `LUKE'S SHORTER OUR FATHER.` · `IMPORTUNITY: SHAMELESS KNOCKING.` · `HOW MUCH MORE THE GOOD SPIRIT.` · then, large: `KNOCK, AND IT SHALL BE OPENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask once more for something. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've asked for before and given up on: healing for someone, a change in yourself, an answer that never came. Let it come back to mind without embarrassment. The man in the story wasn't embarrassed. If you pray, ask for it again, plainly, one more time, and then ask for the good Spirit too. If you don't pray, hold the hope out in front of you again for a moment, as if you were knocking on a door. The bell holds the time.
importunity. The shameless pestering that got the midnight friend his bread, after the disciples asked Jesus, teach us to pray. Today's word.
Your line: knock. Today, whatever you have quietly stopped asking for, ask one more time, plainly, like a neighbor at midnight. Day four hundred sixty-one.

462.title: Blessed the womb (Luke 11:27–28)
462.hook: a woman praises his mother; he says blessed are they who hear the word and keep it; Catholics see Mary as both
462.howItsDone: Catholics read Luke 11:27–28 on some feasts and Saturday Masses of Our Lady, and many pray the rosary as a way of pondering the Gospel's words with Mary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disciples asked to be taught to pray, and a man's importunity kept him knocking at midnight. Your line was knock. Did you ask once more? Day four hundred sixty-two, the end of a week.

You've heard someone do this. A son gives a great speech at a wedding, and an aunt in the crowd calls out: your mother must be so proud! It's a compliment to him, routed through her. Something just like that happens in Luke. Jesus is in the middle of a tense argument with people who say he heals by the power of devils. He's answering them, and a woman in the crowd can't hold it in. She lifts up her voice and calls out a blessing on his mother. It's two verses long. Today, what she said, and what he said back.
screen: `YOUR MOTHER MUST BE SO PROUD.` → `A VOICE FROM THE CROWD.` → `TWO VERSES LONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the woman's cry in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed is the womb that bore thee, and the paps that gave thee suck." Paps is an old word for breasts. It's an earthy, motherly blessing, the kind women in that world gave: how happy the mother of such a son. And Jesus answers: "Yea rather, blessed are they who hear the word of God, and keep it." Some people hear that as a brush-off of his mother. Catholics hear something else, and Luke gives the reason. Go back to the beginning of this Gospel. When the angel came, Mary said be it done to me according to thy word. She heard the word and accepted it. At Bethlehem, Luke says, Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. When she visits Elizabeth, Elizabeth says blessed art thou that hast believed. And in her own song, Mary says all generations shall call me blessed. So in Luke, Mary is the woman from the crowd's blessing and the answer's blessing at once. She bore him, and she heard and kept the word. Augustine said it this way, in his own words: Mary was more blessed in receiving Christ by faith than in conceiving him in the flesh. Notice what that does. Jesus takes a blessing that only one woman in history could have, and opens it to everyone listening. Nobody else can be his mother. Anybody can hear and keep. Which is why Catholics honor Mary as the first disciple, not only as a mother: she shows what keeping looks like.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one word today. Settle, and breathe. Think back over this week's lines: go in peace, nothing for the journey, no looking back, peace be to this house, knock. Let one of them choose you. Say it slowly inside a few times, the way Mary pondered. Don't analyze it. Just keep it, like a stone in your pocket you keep touching. If you pray, ask to keep it the way she did. The bell holds the time.
Blessed the womb. A woman's cry from the crowd praising Jesus' mother, and his answer: blessed are those who hear the word and keep it, as Mary did. Today's word.

Your line: hear and keep it. Carry your one word all day. And that's week sixty-six: she loved much, the women who funded him, take nothing, he set his face, the seventy-two, teach us to pray, and the womb. Day four hundred sixty-two.

fork.setup: a woman in the crowd calls out a blessing on your mother. how does Jesus answer?
options: thank her and move on.
say rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.
say his mother isn't to be praised.
fork.reveal: he widens the blessing to everyone who hears and keeps the word, and Luke has already shown Mary doing exactly that.

original.note: Greek: blessed, happy, the beatitude word. The woman uses it of the womb, and Jesus answers with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus brushed off a compliment to his mother.
what it means: he opens a blessing only Mary could have to everyone who hears and keeps the word, which Luke shows Mary doing too.
what a scholar hears: Luke uses keep (phylasso, and at Bethlehem syntereo) to tie Mary to the ideal hearer; menounge, yea rather, can mean yes, and even more.
